In summary, our research is concerned with
the misincorporation and excision repair of dUMP, a process that is likely to be of considerable importance in the development of resistance to antifolates in vivo.
the effects of antifolates on the incorporation of deoxyuridylate in DNA, and on the subsequent repair of this misincorporated nucleotide.
the consequences of antifolates on the incorporation of dU into DNA and on the subsequent fate of the newly replicated DNA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the incorporation of misincorporation products into DNA, in the absence of new replication, may not be a significant factor in determining the extent of cell kill by antifolate drugs.
the misincorporation and degradation of dUMP in DNA is a major consequence of exposure to BW301U and other antifolate agents.
misincorporation and excision-repair of dUMP are major cellular processes in human cells exposed to lipid soluble antifolates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BW301U is a potent inhibitor of DNA replication, and misincorporation occurs in human cells exposed to the drug, but the misincorporated nucleotide is rapidly removed from newly replicated DNA.
BW301U, like other antifolates, inhibits dTMP synthesis and that this inhibition is followed by misincorporation and subsequent degradation of [3H]-dU in newly replicated DNA.
the misincorporation and excision-repair of misincorporated deoxyuridine are the major pathways by which cells exposed to antifolates avoid lethal DNA damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the misincorporation process is not a consequence of the inhibition of DNA synthesis, but rather is an independent process.
the misincorporation and excision-repair of dUMP in DNA is not a major cause of cell death during treatment with BW301U.
misincorporation is a major consequence of antifolate-induced inhibition of thymidylate synthesis in human cells.
